fields.title: Grifel: requested for two years, nobody uses it
fields.summary: The custom report builder was the top request. Three months later, only 11% use it. Decide what to do.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you do with the report builder?
fields.brief/role: You are a product manager at Grifel.
fields.brief/company: Grifel is a fictional time-tracking service for retail chains: 2,100 corporate clients.
fields.brief/context: The report builder was the top request for two years: 340 votes in the feedback portal, mentioned in 47 deals. It shipped three months ago after a quarter of development. Only 11% of companies use it, and 62% of those built exactly one report and never returned. The Head of Product asks whether to invest further or drop it. The team is split: half think it needs better visibility, half think the request wasn't real.
fields.brief/objective: Determine what to do with the report builder before the next planning cycle.
fields.brief/constraints: Two weeks. The researcher has four days. New analytics tracking can be added, but data will only arrive in a week.
fields.brief/task: Decide what you will do and justify your decision.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Votes represent jobs, not technical specifications
fields.learnTakeaway/body: People describe their tasks in feature requests, but we hear a tool. Twelve ready-made reports and the correct date range solve the exact same problem the builder was meant for—and can be tested in two weeks. Also, distinguish between two conclusions: "the tool isn't being used" speaks about the solution, while "the task isn't needed" speaks about the people—and the second almost never follows from the first.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Support tickets regarding the report builder since launch — 61.

Breakdown from the Head of Support:
— "How to get store hours for last week" — 22. All describe reports that the report builder can build.
— "Report is empty or incorrect" — 17. Comment: "Almost all of it is confusion over date ranges. We default to a calendar month, but people expect their pay period week."
— "Can this be emailed on a schedule" — 14. Not supported.
— Other — 8.

Account manager note: "When I do a screen share and build the report together with them, everything works out in three minutes and the client is happy."
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
A researcher re-read 340 votes and 118 comments attached to them.

Summary:
— 54 comments describe a specific report: "weekly hours by store," "overtime by store manager," "absences by location." Twelve reports cover 41 out of 54.
— 38 — about exporting: people need data exported into a spreadsheet or their own analytics system.
— 14 — about scheduling and email delivery.
— 12 — general: "more reports," "better reports."

The word "builder" does not appear in a single comment: we made it up.
fields.evidenceCards/3/title: A day in the life of a customer
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Reports are needed in two situations: closing a payroll period (once every week or two) and investigating a specific store manager complaint.

In the first case, the user knows exactly what they need and does it on the same day of the week.

For 78% of clients, the payroll period does not coincide with the calendar month.

After generating a report, it is almost always exported to a spreadsheet: for 84% of saved reports, the first run is followed by an export within a minute.

There is no separate event for "report re-opened from bookmark" in analytics tracking.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Interpret requests as jobs and provide ready-made reports
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Treat the 340 votes as requests for specific reports rather than a custom builder: ship the twelve most common as one-click templates and see if people use them.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
Twelve templates cover 41 out of 54 specific requests and can be built in two weeks—the report builder already has all the functionality under the hood, it just needs one-click entry points.
At the same time, you fix the date range: default to the client's payroll period rather than the calendar month. This resolves 17 tickets about "empty or incorrect reports" and, more importantly, addresses the same silent issue for those who didn't write in.
A month later, 38% of companies generate a report at least once instead of 11%, and 19% run them repeatedly.
The next step becomes clear as well: 84% export to spreadsheets, meaning the real job is "getting data out," and email scheduling is intentionally added to the roadmap.
Trade-off: the builder itself remains unloved, and part of the team feels a quarter was wasted—a fact you acknowledge out loud.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Talk to those who opened and abandoned it
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Spend four days of researcher time on eight to ten interviews with companies that opened the report builder but did not save a report, then decide.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
The calls paint a clear picture in four days: people come in with a specific report in mind, assemble it, see figures outside their payroll period, and decide that "it doesn't work."
This confirms what was already in the 61 support tickets and 118 comments—meaning a week was spent confirming readily available insights.
However, one detail emerges that wasn't in the data: half of the interviewees didn't realize a report could be saved and reused—they rebuild it every time.
You enter planning with a diagnosis, but without any built solution.
Trade-off: the right method applied to a question that already had an answer; but it revealed something invisible in the metrics.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Make the report builder more visible
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: 34% open it, 11% reach report creation—meaning people don't understand how to use it. Build an onboarding tour on first launch.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
The tour launches in two weeks. The share of people opening it grows from 34% to 41%, and those creating a report from 11% to 13%.
Inside the builder, nothing changes: 71% were already adding fields, and 44% reached preview—people weren't lost in the UI, they were getting the wrong date range.
Tickets saying "report is empty or incorrect" stay at the same level.
A month later, the team discusses a second onboarding tour.
Trade-off: "getting the wrong thing" was mistaken for "not understanding how"; onboarding increased entry into a tool people were already opening.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Declare the request fake and move on
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Two years of feature requests yielded 11%. Leave the feature running, stop investing, and move on to something else.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The team pivots, and in the moment it looks sensible: feature requests indeed failed to predict usage.
However, 22 tickets asking "how to get store hours" keep coming in, and support continues to handle them manually—taking three minutes per ticket and leaving the customer satisfied.
Six months later, the same request comes from two large retail chains up for renewal, and the topic is reopened under pressure.
Trade-off: from "the tool flopped," you concluded "the job isn't needed," even though these are different statements, and distinguishing them required just a day of reading comments.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: The customer is described through demographics rather than jobs and pain points
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Collected findings were not synthesized, leaving blind spots hidden
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Behavior is explained by persona profile rather than situation
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Failed to identify how the person currently solves the task and why that habit persists
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: The end-to-end journey was not considered: steps outside the product remained invisible
fields.rubric/remediation/5/gap: The root cause is sought at the storefront, though it originates in back-of-house processes
fields.rubric/remediation/6/gap: Hypotheses are shuffled in circles instead of decomposing metrics and breakdowns
fields.rubric/remediation/7/gap: An aggregate metric is evaluated without cohorts, even though audience composition is changing
fields.rubric/remediation/8/gap: Effect size was not estimated prior to execution
